warmup.q: A team's test starts three copies of a payments program on one laptop and stops the one in charge, the leader. Then it checks that no payment reported as saved has gone missing. It has passed 500 times. What has it shown?
options: The switch to a new leader is correct
The switch survives crashes, but not a network that splits
It survived the timings those 500 runs happened to hit, and none of those runs can be replayed exactly
Nothing at all: tests can't find bugs in programs spread over several computers
warmup.why: Each run stopped the leader at whatever moment the laptop, the network and Java happened to produce. The dangerous moments, such as a stop between saving a payment and copying it, or a pause just longer than a timeout, may never have come up. And had one run failed, you couldn't have rerun that exact timing. The second option claims more than the test says: it tells you nothing about a split network either way. The test is still worth keeping. This lesson is about tools that search those timings on purpose.

sections.h: Bugs in rare timings: why 500 passing runs prove little
sections.html:
In 2014, engineers at Amazon described a bug in DynamoDB, the database service Amazon rents to other companies. It could lose data. It needed a particular run of failures and recovery steps mixed in with ordinary work, and the shortest such run was 35 steps long. It had passed careful reviews of the design and the code, and plenty of testing.

Most bugs in distributed systems, programs spread over several computers, have that shape. (Each computer in one is called a node.) The code works in nearly every run and fails only in a few schedules. A schedule is the exact order and timing of everything in one run: each message, each crash, each pause. The bug needs a message delayed just past a timeout, or a pause that starts just after a write and ends just after another computer took over.

An ordinary test runs one schedule, whichever one your laptop, Java and the network happened to produce that time. Run it 500 times on the server that runs a team's tests after every change, and you've tried 500 schedules near the common case. If one fails, you can't run that schedule again. It's the drive round the block.

Network partitions are cheap to cause, and few teams do it. In a partition, the network splits the computers into groups that can't reach each other. In a 2018 paper, Alquraan and colleagues studied 136 failures caused by partitions in 25 widely used systems. Most were catastrophic: lost data, deleted data coming back, broken locks. 88% could be triggered by cutting off a single computer, and 62% were deterministic: once the partition happened, the failure followed. Their tool, NEAT, found 32 new failures in seven systems.

So testing a distributed system means searching schedules and faults on purpose. Teams have settled on layers, each answering a different question (the figure):

  • model checkers such as TLA+ and P check the design, in every schedule of a small model;
  • deterministic simulation checks the real code, in millions of runs you can replay;
  • Jepsen-style testing (named after a project that breaks databases on purpose) checks the real system from outside;
  • property-based tests check one part of the program, on inputs the computer makes up;
  • chaos experiments check the live system, people included.

Car makers test in layers too. The engineer's calculation covers every case on paper, for the car as drawn: the model checker. The crash lab hits the real car from every angle and films it, so any crash replays frame by frame: simulation. A safety agency buys a car from a showroom and crashes it its own way: Jepsen. A bench test of one seat belt is a property test, and a supervised drive in traffic is a chaos experiment.

The rest of this lesson takes the layers in turn, starting with the one that checks a design before any code exists.

try.title: Search seeds for the lost write
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It runs the lab's primary-backup protocol, a set of rules for two computers that keep copies of one value. n1, the primary, takes each write from the client, copies it to n2, the backup, and says "saved" (acknowledges the write) only once n2 confirms. If n2 hears nothing from n1 for 100 ms, it takes over.

The demo runs this on seed after seed. A seed is a number that decides every random choice in one run: each message's delay, and at most one fault (a pause of n1, a cut link between n1 and n2, or a crash of n1). It stops at the first run that loses an acknowledged write.
Before it prints, predict: will the first failure be a crash, a pause or a cut link? Will running the same seed again give the same events?
Read the last events. Which message did the damage, and when had it been sent?
try.expect:
Searching seeds 0 to 9,999 for a run where the naive protocol loses an acknowledged write...
seed 4 fails after 576 events. Fault: Cut(at=809, forMs=175)
  at 1013 ms n2 is the primary and holds 19, but write 20 was acknowledged

The last events before it (heartbeats left out):
    949  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=37, value=19, epoch=1)  DROPPED (link cut)
    951  client -> n2 Read(op=38)
    961  n2 -> client ReadOk(op=38, value=19)
    976  client -> n2 Write(op=39, value=20)
    978  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=37, value=19, epoch=1)  DROPPED (link cut)
    979  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=37, value=19, epoch=1)  DROPPED (link cut)
    984  link n1-n2 healed
    984  n2 -> client Ack(op=39)
    996  client -> n2 Read(op=40)
   1005  n2 -> client ReadOk(op=40, value=20)
   1013  n1 -> n2 Replicate(op=37, value=19, epoch=1)
   1013  VIOLATION: at 1013 ms n2 is the primary and holds 19, but write 20 was acknowledged

Replaying seed 4: 190 trace lines, identical to the first run: true

The fixed protocol (epochs) on the same 10,000 seeds: 0 failures.
That was 15,000 simulated seconds in 3,507 ms of real time.

Seeds 0 to 3 pass and seed 4 fails. In the trace, times are in simulated milliseconds, op numbers each client request, and write k stores the value k. Cut(at=809, forMs=175) is the fault: the link between n1 and n2 is cut at 809 ms for 175 ms. n2 hears nothing, takes over and acknowledges write 20. When the link heals, n1's resend of write 19 arrives, a write n1 accepted during the cut and never got confirmed, and it overwrites n2's 20. The replay matches event for event, which is what makes a seed a bug report. The real time on the last line depends on your machine (a few seconds on a laptop); the simulated time doesn't.

sections.h: Checking the design before the code: model checkers, TLA+ and P
sections.html:
The explorer from the last lesson, System models, is a model checker. You give it a model of a design, meaning the states the system can be in and the steps between them, and a rule. It visits every state it can reach, and returns a shortest list of steps that breaks the rule.

TLA+, a language for describing designs made by Leslie Lamport, is the version real teams use. You describe the design as variables, a starting state and actions, where each action says how one step may change the variables. TLC, the TLA+ model checker, explores every reachable state of a small version, say 3 nodes and at most 2 crashes, and checks your rules in each. Here's the election from the last lesson, where three nodes vote for a leader and a restart can make a node forget its vote. It starts where both candidates have voted for themselves:

\* a sketch of two actions and the rule, not a complete spec
Vote(v, c) ==                               \* node v votes for candidate c
    /\ up[v] /\ votedFor[v] = Nil
    /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![v] = c]
    /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![c] = @ \cup {v}]
    /\ UNCHANGED up

Restart(v) ==                               \* crash-recovery, vote kept in memory
    /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![v] = Nil]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<up, votes>>

OneLeader == \A a, b \in Candidates :
    Cardinality(votes[a]) >= 2 /\ Cardinality(votes[b]) >= 2 => a = b

It reads like this. /\ means "and". A name with a tick, like votedFor', is the variable's value after the step; without the tick, it's the value before. [votedFor EXCEPT ![v] = c] means "the same as before, except that v's entry is now c", and @ \cup {v} adds v to the old set. Nil means no vote, and UNCHANGED up keeps up as it was. So Vote(v, c) says: if v is up and hasn't voted, v votes for c, and c's set of votes gains v. Restart(v) wipes v's memory of its vote. OneLeader is the rule. It reads "for any two candidates a and b, if both have at least 2 votes (Cardinality is the size of a set), then a is b". TLC would find the double vote in three steps: Vote(n2, n1), Restart(n2), Vote(n2, n3).

Amazon's 2014 report is the best evidence that this pays outside universities. By then TLA+ had been used on 10 large systems by 7 teams. Engineers from new hires to the most senior learned it well enough for useful results in 2 to 3 weeks. The 939-line description of DynamoDB's replication, the way it copies data between computers, found the 35-step bug and two others. A network algorithm in S3, Amazon's file storage service, had 2 bugs in 804 lines. EBS, its disk service, had 3 bugs in only 102 lines.

P is the other modelling language at Amazon. It describes a system as state machines, parts that are always in one of a few named states and move between them as messages arrive. Its checker tries the orders of those messages, and failures, systematically. A tool called PObserve checks logs from test and live runs against the P description afterwards.

Model checking has two limits. The model is small on purpose, and the number of states grows fast: the Try it shows the fixed election going from 268 states to 151,320 when it grows from 3 nodes and 1 crash to 5 nodes and 2. A bug that needs a bigger model or a longer run stays hidden. And the description isn't the code. The design can be right while the Kotlin has a bug, and the two drift apart as the code changes. PObserve narrows that gap. The next layer closes it from the other side, by testing the real code.

try.title: Watch the state space grow
steps: Run the demo below. It explores the fixed election from the last lesson in full, for 3 and 5 nodes and up to 2 crashes. All the states a model can reach make up its state space.
Before it prints, guess how many states 5 nodes with 2 crashes have, given that 3 nodes with 1 crash have 268.
Which grows the state space faster here: one more crash, or two more nodes?

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.dist.l07.demo.ExploreDemoKt -Pargs='grow' --console=plain -q

try.expect:
The fixed election (votes on disk before replying), crash-recovery, explored in full:

nodes  crashes     states      time
    3        0         36     21 ms
    3        1        268      7 ms
    3        2        940      9 ms
    5        0      2,916     21 ms
    5        1     31,060    120 ms
    5        2    151,320    501 ms

Two more nodes multiply the states by 80 to 160; one more crash multiplies them by 3.5 to 11. Every extra node adds messages that can arrive in any order. The times are small and change from run to run. Java speeds code up as it runs it, and the first row pays for that warm-up. Real descriptions hit the same wall sooner. That's why Amazon ran TLC on ten rented computers at once for the DynamoDB description, and why every model is kept small.

sections.h: Deterministic simulation: the real code in a fake world
sections.html:
Remember seed 4 from the first Try it: it failed, and replaying it gave the same 190 lines. That's deterministic simulation testing (DST): run the real code, many times, in a world the test controls. Everything that could differ between two runs goes through two things. One is a random number generator started from a seed: it makes numbers that look random but come from a formula, so the same seed always gives the same numbers. The other is a virtual clock, a pretend clock that only the test moves forward.

The seed decides which message arrives next and when, which disk write fails, and when a computer crashes or pauses. Nothing sleeps: the clock jumps straight to the next event. A run is then decided entirely by its seed. Try seed after seed and check the rules after every event. When one fails, the seed is a complete bug report: run it again and the same thing happens at the same simulated millisecond, even under a debugger, a tool that pauses a program to inspect it.

The lab builds a small one, for the primary-backup protocol from the first Try it. The primary, n1, applies a write, waits for the backup's confirmation, then acknowledges the client. A backup that hears nothing for 100 ms promotes itself: it becomes the primary and tells the registry, a small directory that tells the client where to send requests. The simulator allows message delays of 1 to 10 ms, and one fault per run on n1: a pause, a cut link or a crash.

The stepper shows seed 36. n1 pauses for 172 ms, n2 promotes itself and acknowledges write 10, and n1 wakes still believing it's the primary. Its late copy of write 9 overwrites n2's 10. Crashes alone never cause it, because a computer that stops for good can't come back and do damage. The fix is the fencing token from Leases, locks and fencing tokens: an epoch, a number that each new primary raises and the old one can't match.

FoundationDB, a database that Apple uses, was built this way from its first line. Everything that could differ between runs (network, disk, time, random numbers) sits behind a layer the simulator replaces. So a whole cluster and its test run inside one program, one event at a time. The code also cooperates through buggification: at chosen points it may return an unusual error, add a delay or pick an odd setting, so that rare paths run often. Because the simulated clock skips idle time, slow bugs show up fast. Apple's CloudKit, which stores data for iPhone apps, has run FoundationDB for more than 0.5 million disk-years without a data corruption event. (One disk running for a year is a disk-year.)

TigerBeetle's simulator, the VOPR, runs a group of real TigerBeetle servers under network, disk and crash faults at 1000 times real speed, around the clock, on 1,024 processor cores.

The price is how true to life the fake world is. The FoundationDB paper names the limits: simulation can't find performance problems, can't test outside libraries or code outside its framework, and can't catch an operating system that behaves differently from what the simulator assumes.

A failure you can't replay is a rumour. Make every run a function of its seed.

So the simulator can only be as cruel as its authors imagined. Next, we'll meet the layer that tests the real system from outside, with no simulator at all.

frames.say: The same seed and pause with the fix. n2 promoted itself into epoch 2, and the first heartbeat (an "I'm alive" message) from n2 that n1 handles makes n1 step down. The Replicates n1 sent a moment earlier carry epoch 1, so n2 refuses them and keeps 10. This is lesson 5's fencing token, checked by the computer that holds the data.

sections.h: Testing the real system from outside: Jepsen and Elle
sections.html:
A simulator tests only the code you can put inside it. Jepsen, the testing library Kyle Kingsbury wrote, tests the system as people really run it: the real programs, on real or virtual machines, over a real network. He also publishes what he finds. It's black-box testing: it judges the system only by what its clients saw, never by looking inside.

A test has four parts. A generator makes up reads and writes for many clients running at once. A nemesis causes faults while they run. It splits the network with firewall rules, filters that block traffic between chosen computers. It kills and pauses programs, changes clocks, and fakes power cuts that lose every write that hadn't reached the disk (with LazyFS, a stand-in for the layer that stores files).

Every operation goes into a history twice: once when it starts, and once when it ends. It ends as ok (it happened), fail (it certainly didn't), or info, when the client can't tell, as after the timeouts of Partial failure, lesson 1 of this track. Then a checker asks whether any order of those operations fits the promise the database makes.

Elle is Jepsen's checker for transactions, groups of reads and writes that a database promises to treat as one unit (the Transactions track). In its favourite test, each write adds a unique item to the end of a list, so every read shows the order of all the writes before it. From that, Elle works out which transaction must have come before which, and looks for a loop: A before B, and B before A. Each loop is one of the anomalies from the Transactions track, the named ways that transactions running at once can see each other's half-done work.

The results keep humbling well-tested systems. Jepsen's 2025 analysis of TigerBeetle 0.16.11, a database designed around its simulator, found two safety bugs and seven crashes. Queries with several filters could leave out results, and a debugging feature of the Java client (the library Java programs use to talk to TigerBeetle) returned wrong times. Two crashes came from single flipped bits: in padding (spare bytes that line data up) and in the superblock (the block that says where everything is on disk).

The VOPR had missed them because it damaged whole sectors, the fixed-size pieces a disk reads and writes. A damaged sector fails its checksum, a short number stored with the data to spot changes, and gets repaired from another copy, so the code that checks padding never ran. The query bug escaped four fuzzers, programs that throw random inputs at code, because none of them made data that sends a query down that rare path. A simulator finds only the faults its authors thought to cause, and the work they thought to generate.

Jepsen still credited TigerBeetle's simulation for much of its safety, and reminded readers that tests like these can show bugs exist, never that none do.

A black-box checker sees only what clients saw, and that hides damage. The lab's naive protocol loses a write in 1,559 of 10,000 runs, but a client's read shows it in only 883. In the rest, a newer write covers the damage before anyone reads, or the client has already stopped. That's why Jepsen tests usually heal the network at the end and read everything back.

Jepsen needs real machines and real time. The last layers are smaller, and you can run them with every change.

Seed 10 (Cut(at=244, forMs=216)), the client's history around the first stale read:
   op  kind  value  invoked  completed  attempts
    9  write     5   188 ms     214 ms         1

sections.h: Smaller layers: fault injection, chaos experiments and property tests
sections.html:
Say the payments program asks the card company to approve a payment, and one day the reply takes 1,100 ms instead of 100. What does your code do? Fault injection in everyday tests finds out, by putting a misbehaving network between your code and a real program it depends on. Toxiproxy is a small program for that: it sits on the connection and passes the bytes along, slowly or not at all when told to. Testcontainers, a Java library that starts real programs in containers (small, separate systems on your computer) for a test, has it ready: the module org.testcontainers:testcontainers-toxiproxy:2.0.5 starts the image ghcr.io/shopify/toxiproxy:2.5.0.

A test adds a toxic, Toxiproxy's word for one kind of trouble, such as 1,100 ms of delay on replies, or a speed of 0 to cut the connection. Then it checks what your code does. Does the timeout fire? Does the retry carry the same idempotency key, the unique number that lets the other side spot a repeat? Does the code stop calling a program that keeps failing? You choose one fault at a time, which is both the strength and the limit.

Chaos engineering runs experiments on the live system, on purpose. Chaos Monkey, which switched off servers at random at Netflix, the film-streaming company, made it famous. The Principles of Chaos Engineering describe something more careful. Pick a number that shows the system is healthy, its steady state, such as payments per minute. Predict that it holds in a control group, left alone, and in an experimental group. Cause one real-world event in the experimental group, look for a difference, and keep the blast radius, the part that can be harmed, small. It's the only layer that tests the alarms, the written instructions and the people who respond, and the wrong place to look for a lost write.

Property-based testing makes up the inputs. You state a property, such as "no acknowledged write is ever lost", and a library tries hundreds of made-up cases. When one fails, it shrinks it: it tries smaller versions until it finds the smallest that still fails. In the lab, jqwik 1.10.2, a property-testing library for Java and Kotlin, makes up the fault itself. It shrinks a failure to something like "a pause of n1 at 100 ms for 133 ms", which reads as a bug report. Kotest, a testing library for Kotlin, does the same with checkAll. Unlike a seed, jqwik knows what a fault looks like, so it can make one smaller.

No single method is enough, because each one checks something the others can't. The car picture breaks in one place: a crash lab, like a simulator, can only stage crashes someone imagined, while real roads, and real networks, keep inventing new ones.

One passing layer says nothing about the others. Test in layers.

Method Checks Misses
TLA+, P the design, in every schedule of a small model bugs in the code; bugs that need a bigger model
Deterministic simulation the real code, in millions of runs that replay faults and work nobody put in the simulator
Jepsen and Elle the real system, under real faults damage no client saw; it can't prove there are no bugs
Property-based tests one part of the program, on made-up inputs problems between parts
Fault injection, chaos your code, and the people running it, under one real fault rare combinations of faults

opening:
Your car makes a strange knock, but only on cold mornings, and only when you turn left out of the driveway. You take it to the garage. The mechanic drives it round the block, hears nothing, and hands back the keys: it's fine.

It isn't fine, and the mechanic isn't careless. The drive round the block tried the easy conditions, and the knock needs a rare mix of them. Testing again and again feels like proof, because every pass looks the same.

Programs that run on several computers fail like that knock. In System models, the lab's explorer found two leaders by trying every order of a few steps. Real systems have far too many orders to try them all.

In this lesson, we'll build a fake world where the test controls time and luck, find a lost payment in it and replay it exactly. Then we'll meet the five kinds of testing that teams use, and what each one misses. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a car that knocked only on cold mornings, and a mechanic who drove it round the block. Five hundred passing runs are five hundred drives round the block. The tools in this lesson go looking for the cold morning on purpose.

Open a program you can read, your own or an open-source one, and search it for currentTimeMillis and Random(. Each hit is a place where two runs can differ, and where a simulator would need a seed.

That ends Faults, time and truth. Next, in the Consistency and consensus track, we'll write down the rules a history is checked against: when copies of one balance disagree, which values may a read return?

compare.note: The history on the left is all Jepsen ever has: what each client asked, what came back, and when. From it, a checker can prove something went wrong (read 16 can't return 6 after write 8 was acknowledged), but not why. And it misses any damage that no read saw. The trace on the right sees every message and both computers, so it catches the lost write at the event that caused it, and the seed replays it. The price of that view is that it exists only for code running inside the simulator, under the faults someone wrote into it.

worked.title: A deterministic simulator in five moves

steps.say: Send every random choice through one generator made from the seed. Draw the fault first, even when the test passes one in, so the delays that follow come out the same either way.
steps.code: private val rng = Random(seed) private val drawn = Fault.random(rng) // always drawn: keeps the stream of numbers stable val fault: Fault = fault ?: drawn

steps.say: Replace time with a queue of events sorted by virtual time, then by the order they were added. Two events at the same millisecond then always run in the same order.
steps.code: private class Event(val at: Long, val seq: Long, val node: String?, val action: () -> Unit) private val queue = PriorityQueue(compareBy<Event>({ it.at }, { it.seq })) private fun schedule(at: Long, node: String?, action: () -> Unit) { queue += Event(at, seq++, node, action) }

steps.say: Make faults decisions of the event loop, the loop that takes the next event and runs it. A crashed node's events are dropped. A paused node's events wait until it wakes, in their original order.
steps.code: val e = queue.poll() now = e.at if (e.node != null && e.node in down) continue // crashed: does nothing val wake = e.node?.let { pausedUntil[it] } if (wake != null && now < wake) { schedule(wake, e.node, e.action); continue } // paused: later e.action()

steps.say: Check the rule after every event, with the god's-eye view of both computers that a real test never has.
steps.code: val primary = servers.getValue(registry) if (primary.value < highestAcked) violation = "at $now ms ${primary.name} holds ${primary.value}, but write $highestAcked was acknowledged"

steps.say: Search seeds and keep the first failure. Replaying it means running the same seed again.
steps.code: fun search(seeds: LongRange, protocol: Protocol): Run? { for (seed in seeds) { val run = Simulation(seed, protocol).run() if (run.violation != null) return run // the seed is the bug report } return null }

lab.title: A seeded simulator that catches a zombie primary
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 8 fail: 6 in SimulationTest and 2 jqwik properties in NoLostWritePropertyTest. If you haven't done the last Try it yet, read the jqwik failure now: it's the naive protocol's bug, already shrunk.

Read Simulation.kt from the top. It's finished apart from one line: the event queue, the network, the faults, the client and the god's-eye check are given. Read NaivePrimaryBackup in PrimaryBackup.kt too, and find the line marked as the bug.
In Dst.kt, write search (exercise 1). Run --tests 'sfz.dist.l08.SimulationTest': the search finds a failing seed, but the tests that replay a seed still fail.
Exercise 2: one line in Simulation.kt draws a random number without the seed. Find it and fix it, and the replay tests pass.

Exercise 3: give PrimaryBackup epochs, as the comment above it describes, so that a zombie primary (an old primary that wakes up still acting in charge) can't overwrite the new one. Run all 8 tests. The fixed protocol must survive 2,000 seeds and 600 faults made up by jqwik.
hints: search is a for loop over seeds that returns the first Simulation(seed, protocol, faultFor?.invoke(seed)).run() whose violation isn't null.
Exercise 2: look at how send picks a delay. Random.nextLong uses Random.Default, which starts from a different seed in every run of Java; the simulation's own generator is rng.

Exercise 3: write one helper, admit(theirs: Int): Boolean, for every message from the other computer. Answer Refused(epoch) and return false if theirs < epoch; adopt theirs and step down if it's larger; then set lastHeard and return true.
Promotion is epoch += 1 next to isPrimary = true. Every Replicate and Heartbeat sends epoch, and stepping down clears waiting, so the old primary never acknowledges those writes.
If a deposed primary steps down fails, check that your step-down calls env.log with the words steps down.

drill.title: Write the simulator's loop from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the main loop of a simulator that jumps from event to event. Events are sorted by time, then by the order they were added. Skip events for crashed nodes, push a paused node's events to its wake-up time, then run the event and check the rule. Then name two things that would make two runs of the same seed differ.

answer.html: while (queue.isNotEmpty() && violation == null) { val e = queue.poll() // smallest (at, seq) first if (e.at > endAt) break now = e.at // virtual time jumps; nothing sleeps if (e.node != null && e.node in down) continue val wake = e.node?.let { pausedUntil[it] } if (wake != null && now < wake) { // paused: same event, later, order kept by seq schedule(wake, e.node, e.action) continue } e.action() // may send messages, set timers check() // the invariant, after every event } // Two runs of one seed differ if anything bypasses the seed: Random.Default or // System.nanoTime() in the code under test, iteration over a HashSet of objects // with identity hash codes, or a real thread racing the event loop.

recap: Bugs in distributed systems hide in rare schedules: Amazon's DynamoDB bug needed 35 steps, and 88% of the studied partition failures needed only one computer cut off. Ordinary tests try a few schedules and can't replay them.
TLA+ and P check the design in every schedule of a small model (at Amazon: 10 systems, 7 teams, learned in 2 to 3 weeks). They miss bugs in the code, and bugs that need a bigger model.
Deterministic simulation runs the real code with every random choice taken from one seed and a virtual clock, so a failing seed replays exactly (FoundationDB, TigerBeetle's VOPR).

Jepsen judges the real, running system by its client history (each operation's start, then ok, fail or info), and Elle finds loops in the order of transactions. It can show that bugs exist, never that none do.
Toxiproxy tests your code against one real fault, chaos experiments test the live system and its people, and property tests (jqwik, Kotest) shrink a failure to its smallest case. Use several layers.
The limit: every layer finds only the faults and the work it was given. Jepsen found TigerBeetle bugs from single flipped bits that the VOPR, running around the clock, had never caused.

explain.prompt: A team is building a program that keeps a payments app's money records on three computers, using Raft to agree on the order of writes. Someone asks which testing to spend time on. Explain what each layer would catch, and why you'd want more than one.
explain.answer: Start with the design. Check a TLA+ or P model of how the computers copy writes and pick a new leader, on 3 nodes with a couple of crashes. It catches design bugs in every schedule of that small model, such as a vote that isn't saved to disk, or a takeover that loses acknowledged writes. It can't see bugs in our Kotlin. For that, write each computer's logic against a clock, a random generator and a network passed in from outside, and run it in a deterministic simulator. Thousands of seeded runs with crashes, pauses and network splits check the rules after every event, and any failure replays from its seed. The simulator finds only the faults we modelled. So before we trust the real system, run Jepsen-style tests against the real programs, with network splits, kills and power cuts that lose unsaved writes, judged from the client history. Property tests cover single parts, such as the code that turns records into bytes. Toxiproxy in everyday tests checks our timeouts and retries one fault at a time, and chaos experiments on the live system check the alarms and the people. Each layer misses something the others catch, so a pass at one tells us nothing about the rest.

deeper.html:
Determinism at three levels. FoundationDB and TigerBeetle get determinism from how the program is written: one event loop, and every outside effect behind a layer the test can replace. Other projects get it from the runtime, swapping the part that decides which piece of work runs next, under unchanged code. Antithesis, a company that sells this kind of testing, gets it from the machine. Its hypervisor, the program that runs virtual computers, makes ordinary programs repeatable on one core with a virtual clock, even if they were never written for simulation. The trade is effort against fidelity: the higher the level, the less of the real world the simulation sees, and the lower, the slower each run.

On the JVM. You can start without a new tool. Find the code that decides something over time, such as a retry or a lock that must be renewed. Pass it a java.time.Clock and a seeded Random, instead of letting it read the system clock and Random.Default. Write the logic as a reaction to messages and timer events, not threads and sleeps. Then the same code runs for real, and in a simulator test that tries thousands of seeds. kotlinx-coroutines-test's runTest already runs coroutines (Kotlin's lightweight tasks) on a virtual clock that skips delay, so a test of a function that waits 30 seconds finishes at once. It doesn't explore different orders of work, but it removes real sleeps, which is the first step.

Test the simulator. A simulator that isn't deterministic fails quietly. Say a run reads System.currentTimeMillis() deep in a library, walks a HashSet whose order changes from run to run, or lets a second thread race the event loop. Then a failing seed no longer fails on your machine. Run one seed twice on every build and compare the whole trace, as the lab's first test does. When Jepsen, a user or a bad day finds a bug, first make the simulator reproduce it, the way FoundationDB reproduced bugs from the field before debugging them.

Jepsen keeps finding bugs. In March 2026 Jepsen reported lost updates, where one write silently undoes another, in MariaDB Galera Cluster 12.1.2, a database that keeps copies on several computers, even on healthy clusters.

Swarm testing. FoundationDB randomizes not only faults but the whole test: cluster size, settings, the work, fault rates, and which buggification points are on. Runs that are each less thorough, but differ from each other, find more bugs than many runs of one carefully tuned setup.

Elle's anomalies, and a harder check. Elle is fast: its time grows roughly in step with the length of the history, and a history of 22 million transactions checks in about two minutes. It names the loops it finds with the codes used for transaction anomalies: G0, G1c, G-single (read skew) and G2. Jepsen's older checker, Knossos, checks a stronger promise: that the database acts like one copy, updated in real-time order (linearizability, which the Consistency and consensus track opens up). It searches for an order of operations that fits, and that search grows exponentially with the number of clients at once, which limits it to a few hundred operations. Elle avoids the search by choosing work whose reads reveal the order directly, at the cost of not catching everything.

The framing of this lesson (formal methods, fault injection and deterministic simulation as layers that complete each other) follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 9. The lab's primary-backup protocol and its numbers are this course's own.
